question_text: Why does a computer system organize storage as a hierarchy rather than using a single, large, fast memory technology?
options: A. To eliminate the need for virtual memory.
B. To exploit the principle of locality while balancing speed, capacity, and cost.
C. To guarantee that every memory access is a cache hit.
D. To remove the need for an operating system in memory management.
reference_answer: B. To exploit the principle of locality while balancing speed, capacity, and cost.
scoring_points: Correctly identifies locality as the enabling principle.
Recognizes the speed-capacity-cost trade-off.

question_text: Which of the following statements about locality are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A. Temporal locality means that a recently accessed item is likely to be accessed again soon.
B. Spatial locality means that items whose addresses are close to a recently accessed item are likely to be accessed soon.
C. A loop body executed many times is a classic example of spatial locality.
D. Array traversal is a classic example of spatial locality.
scoring_points: Correctly defines temporal locality.
Correctly defines spatial locality.
Correctly classifies the examples (loop is temporal; array traversal is spatial).

question_text: In a direct-mapped cache, a given main-memory block can be placed in any cache block.
scoring_points: Correctly states that a block maps to exactly one cache block in a direct-mapped cache.

question_text: For a 32-bit byte-addressable machine with a 64 KiB direct-mapped cache and 32-byte cache blocks, how many bits are used for the offset, index, and tag fields? Show the calculation briefly.
reference_answer: Offset = 5 bits; index = 11 bits; tag = 16 bits (32 - 5 - 11).
scoring_points: Offset = 5 bits.
Index = 11 bits with correct block-count reasoning.
Tag = 16 bits.
Correct arithmetic throughout.

question_text: A processor has a 2-level cache hierarchy. L1 hit time is 2 ns with a 90% hit rate; L2 hit time (including L1 miss penalty) is 10 ns with an 80% hit rate for accesses that miss in L1; main memory access time is 100 ns. Calculate the Average Memory Access Time (AMAT).
scoring_points: Correct AMAT formula for a multi-level hierarchy.
Correct L1 contribution of 1.8 ns.
Correct L2/memory contribution of 2.8 ns.
Final answer 4.6 ns.

question_text: Which statements about cache write policies are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A. Write-through writes the data to both the cache and the lower-level memory on every write.
B. Write-back writes data to the lower-level memory only when the block is replaced.
C. Write-back typically requires a dirty bit to track whether a block has been modified.
D. Write-through always produces fewer memory writes than write-back.
scoring_points: Correctly describes write-through.
Correctly describes write-back and the role of the dirty bit.
Correctly rejects D (write-through generally produces more lower-level writes).

question_text: A TLB miss necessarily implies a page fault.
scoring_points: Correctly explains that a TLB miss only means the translation is not in the TLB; the page may still be resident in physical memory.

question_text: Explain what happens to cache performance when the working set of a program exceeds the cache capacity. What phenomenon can occur if the working set exceeds physical memory?
reference_answer: Cache hit ratio drops; if the working set exceeds physical memory, the system thrashes (excessive page faults, low CPU utilization).
scoring_points: Cache hit ratio decreases when working set exceeds cache capacity.
Correctly identifies thrashing when working set exceeds physical memory.
Explains that thrashing causes excessive page faults / low CPU utilization.

question_text: Consider the following C code: for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) { sum += A[i][j]; } }. A is a large row-major 2D array and the cache is much smaller than the whole array. Does this loop exhibit good spatial locality? Briefly justify your answer.
reference_answer: Yes, good spatial locality: C stores 2D arrays in row-major order, so consecutive j values access consecutive addresses in the same row.
scoring_points: States yes / good spatial locality.
Correctly invokes row-major layout.
Correctly explains why contiguous access matters for spatial locality.

question_text: Why do modern processors use multiple levels of cache (L1, L2, L3) instead of a single large cache? Give two distinct reasons.
reference_answer: Speed vs. capacity trade-off (a single large cache has longer hit time); cost/area (SRAM is expensive); filtering effect (L2/L3 capture L1 misses).
scoring_points: Reason 1: speed-capacity trade-off / hit-time concern.
Reason 2: cost, area, or filtering effect.
